sat-readiness-check-reading-and-writing-.prompt: In many coastal towns, oyster reefs were harvested until little of them remained. Restoration groups now return empty shells to the water so that young oysters have a hard surface on which to settle. Within a few years, the rebuilt reefs filter water, shelter small fish, and soften the force of storm waves reaching the shore. Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

options.a: Restored oyster reefs provide several environmental benefits once young oysters settle on the returned shells.
options.b: Oyster harvesting has been banned in coastal towns because the reefs protect the shoreline from storm waves.
options.c: Young oysters can settle only on shells that come from the same reef where the older oysters once lived.
options.d: Small fish depend on oyster reefs for shelter more than they depend on any other kind of coastal habitat.

sat-readiness-check-reading-and-writing-.explanation: Main-idea questions reward the choice that covers the whole text. The text moves from the loss of reefs to shell restoration to the payoff (cleaner water, fish habitat, storm protection), so the main idea is that restored reefs bring several benefits.

distractorExplanations.b: The text never says harvesting was banned; it describes restoration, and storm protection is only one benefit.
distractorExplanations.c: The text says shells give oysters a hard surface; it never limits settling to shells from the same reef.
distractorExplanations.d: Sheltering fish is one benefit listed, but the text makes no comparison with other coastal habitats.

sat-readiness-check-reading-and-writing-.prompt: Architectural historian Lena Brandt notes that the first department stores of the 1850s were designed less like shops than like theaters: grand staircases, glass domes, and long sightlines invited shoppers to linger and watch one another. Brandt argues that this design turned buying into a public event, and that later shopping malls borrowed the same idea when they placed fountains and food courts at their centers. Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

options.a: Brandt claims that early department stores used theatrical design to make shopping a social spectacle, an idea later malls copied.
options.b: Brandt claims that modern malls attract fewer visitors than early department stores did because designers abandoned grand features.
options.c: Brandt claims that early department stores were built inside former theaters, which explains their staircases and domes.
options.d: Brandt claims that shoppers in the 1850s preferred watching performances in department stores to buying the goods on sale.

sat-readiness-check-reading-and-writing-.explanation: The text says stores were designed 'like theaters' so that shopping became a public event, and that malls later reused the idea with fountains and food courts. Only this choice captures both the claim about early stores and the link to malls.

distractorExplanations.b: The text compares design ideas, not visitor numbers; it says malls borrowed the idea rather than abandoned it.
distractorExplanations.d: Shoppers watched one another, not staged performances, and the text never says they avoided buying.
distractorExplanations.c: Misreads the comparison: the stores were designed like theaters, not built inside actual theaters.

sat-readiness-check-reading-and-writing-.prompt: For decades, biologists assumed that the bright colors of poison dart frogs evolved mainly to warn predators that the frogs are toxic. A team led by herpetologist Ana Ruiz found that, in some populations, the brightest males also win more mates, and that females prefer brighter partners even when no predators are present in the test tanks. Ruiz concludes that warning and mate choice may have reinforced each other in shaping the frogs' coloration. Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

options.a: Research suggests that the frogs' bright colors may be shaped by mate preference as well as by warning predators.
options.b: Research shows that the frogs' bright colors no longer warn predators and now serve only to attract mates.
options.c: Research suggests that predators are less likely to attack brightly colored frogs that have recently found a mate.
options.d: Research shows that female frogs choose mates mainly by body size, so coloration has little effect on mating.

sat-readiness-check-reading-and-writing-.explanation: Ruiz does not reject the warning explanation; she adds mate choice and says the two forces 'may have reinforced each other.' The correct choice keeps both factors and the hedged 'may,' matching the text's careful conclusion.

distractorExplanations.c: Invents a link between mating and predator attacks that the text never describes.
distractorExplanations.d: Contradicts the text, which says females prefer brighter partners.
distractorExplanations.b: Overstates the finding with 'no longer' and 'only'; the text keeps warning as one cause.

sat-readiness-check-reading-and-writing-.prompt: The following text is from a short story. Marisol had driven past the old cannery every day for years without noticing it. That morning, though, fog had settled over the harbor, and the building's rusted roof rose out of the gray like the hull of a ship. She slowed the car, surprised to feel that something she had ignored for so long now seemed to be waiting for her. Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

options.a: Marisol decides to buy the old cannery after realizing that it could be turned into a museum.
options.b: Marisol is frightened by the thick fog and pulls over until it is safe to keep driving.
options.c: Marisol remembers working at the cannery as a child and is saddened that it has fallen apart.
options.d: A change in the weather leads Marisol to see a familiar building in a new and striking way.

sat-readiness-check-reading-and-writing-.explanation: The text contrasts years of ignoring the cannery with one foggy morning when it suddenly looks like a ship and seems to be 'waiting for her.' The main idea is the shift in how she perceives a familiar place, triggered by the fog.

distractorExplanations.a: Nothing in the text mentions buying the building or turning it into a museum.
distractorExplanations.b: She slows down because she is struck by the building, not because she is afraid of the fog.
distractorExplanations.c: The text gives no memory of working at the cannery; it stresses that she had never noticed it.

sat-readiness-check-reading-and-writing-.prompt: Urban planner Theo Mensah studied a city that replaced several downtown parking lots with small parks. He found that weekday foot traffic on nearby streets rose by nearly a third, and that cafés and bookstores next to the new parks reported higher sales than similar shops elsewhere downtown. According to the text, what did Mensah find about the shops next to the new parks?

options.a: They reported higher sales than comparable shops in other parts of downtown.
options.b: They lost customers because drivers could no longer find parking spaces nearby.
options.c: They extended their opening hours to serve the larger weekend crowds in the parks.
options.d: They helped pay for the new parks in exchange for lower rent from the city.

sat-readiness-check-reading-and-writing-.explanation: Detail questions are answered directly in the text: shops next to the parks 'reported higher sales than similar shops elsewhere downtown.' The correct choice restates that comparison in different words.

distractorExplanations.c: The text discusses weekday foot traffic; it never mentions opening hours or weekend crowds.
distractorExplanations.d: Nothing in the text says the shops funded the parks or received lower rent.
distractorExplanations.b: Contradicts the text, which reports higher sales, not lost customers.

sat-readiness-check-reading-and-writing-.prompt: In her essay on translation, writer Yuki Tanabe describes reading the same short poem in five English versions. One translator kept every image but lost the poem's rhythm; another kept the rhythm but replaced a plum tree with an apple tree. Tanabe concludes that no single translation can carry everything, so serious readers should compare several versions side by side. Based on the text, what does Tanabe recommend?

options.a: Reading more than one translation of a poem to see what each version preserves
options.b: Choosing the translation that keeps a poem's rhythm, since rhythm matters most
options.c: Learning a poem's original language before reading any translated version of it
options.d: Replacing unfamiliar images with familiar ones so that English readers can relate

sat-readiness-check-reading-and-writing-.explanation: Tanabe's recommendation comes in the last sentence: because no single translation carries everything, readers 'should compare several versions side by side.' Reading more than one translation is the same advice.

distractorExplanations.b: She does not rank rhythm above images; she says each version loses something.
distractorExplanations.d: Swapping the plum tree is something one translator did, not something Tanabe recommends.
distractorExplanations.c: Tanabe never says readers must learn the original language first.

sat-readiness-check-reading-and-writing-.prompt: Economists once treated a country's informal sector—street vendors, unregistered repair shops, and similar businesses—as a sign of failed development that would shrink as the economy grew. Recent studies paint a more complicated picture: in several fast-growing economies, the informal sector has expanded alongside the formal one, often supplying cheap goods and services that formal firms rely on. Such findings suggest that informal work may be a lasting part of growth rather than a stage to be outgrown. Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

options.a: Informal businesses slow economic growth because they compete unfairly with registered firms.
options.b: Governments should register informal businesses so that growth statistics become more accurate.
options.c: Fast-growing economies have eliminated most informal work by offering cheaper formal services.
options.d: New evidence challenges the older view that informal businesses disappear as economies develop.

sat-readiness-check-reading-and-writing-.explanation: The text sets up an old assumption (informal work shrinks with growth) and then presents studies showing informal work expanding with growth. The main idea is that this evidence challenges the older view.

distractorExplanations.a: The text says formal firms rely on informal suppliers; it never claims informal work slows growth.
distractorExplanations.b: The text makes no policy recommendation about registering businesses or fixing statistics.
distractorExplanations.c: Contradicts the text, which says the informal sector expanded in fast-growing economies.

sat-readiness-check-reading-and-writing-.prompt: Many people think of deserts as nearly lifeless, but the Sonoran Desert is one of the most plant-rich deserts in North America. Its two rainy seasons—brief, intense summer storms and gentler winter rains—allow both heat-loving cacti and cool-season wildflowers to thrive in the same landscape. Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

options.a: The Sonoran Desert's two rainy seasons help it support a wide variety of plant life.
options.b: The Sonoran Desert receives more rain each year than any other desert in the world.
options.c: Cacti in the Sonoran Desert grow only during the cool winter rainy season each year.
options.d: Most visitors to the Sonoran Desert are surprised to find that it has no wildflowers.

sat-readiness-check-reading-and-writing-.explanation: The text corrects the idea that deserts are lifeless and explains why the Sonoran Desert is plant-rich: two rainy seasons support both cacti and wildflowers. The correct choice joins the cause (two rainy seasons) to the effect (plant variety).

distractorExplanations.b: The text never compares total rainfall with other deserts; it describes the timing of rain.
distractorExplanations.c: The text calls cacti 'heat-loving' and links the winter rains to wildflowers, not cacti.
distractorExplanations.d: Contradicts the text, which says cool-season wildflowers thrive there.

sat-readiness-check-reading-and-writing-.prompt: Sociologist Dana Whitfield claims that people who volunteer regularly feel more connected to their neighborhoods than people who do not volunteer, even when both groups have lived in the area for the same length of time. Which finding, if true, would most directly support Whitfield's claim?

options.a: Among residents with equal years in the area, volunteers are more likely to say they know and trust their neighbors.
options.b: Volunteers tend to have lived in their neighborhoods for many more years than residents who do not volunteer at all.
options.c: People who move to a new neighborhood often begin volunteering during their first year, before they know many neighbors.
options.d: Most volunteer organizations recruit new members through personal invitations from friends who already live nearby.

sat-readiness-check-reading-and-writing-.explanation: Whitfield's claim has two parts: volunteers feel more connected, and this holds when length of residence is the same. Only the finding that compares residents with equal years in the area and shows volunteers trusting neighbors more tests both parts.

distractorExplanations.c: When people start volunteering says nothing about whether volunteers end up feeling more connected.
distractorExplanations.d: How organizations recruit members does not compare the connectedness of volunteers and non-volunteers.
distractorExplanations.b: This points to a different explanation (longer residence), which the claim specifically rules out.

sat-readiness-check-reading-and-writing-.prompt: In the poem "Field Notes in March," the speaker presents early spring as a time of uneasy waiting rather than joyful renewal. Which quotation from the poem most effectively illustrates this claim?

options.a: "Sunlight spills like honey on the porch, / and every window opens wide."
options.b: "The creek runs loud with melted snow / and carries winter out to sea."
options.c: "The children race across the yard / in coats they no longer need."
options.d: "The ground is soft but will not promise; / we watch the buds and hold our breath."

sat-readiness-check-reading-and-writing-.explanation: The claim stresses uneasy waiting. 'Will not promise' signals uncertainty, and 'we watch the buds and hold our breath' shows tense waiting. The other lines celebrate warmth and renewal, the opposite of the claim.

distractorExplanations.a: Honeyed sunlight and opened windows express the joyful renewal the claim says the poem avoids.
distractorExplanations.b: Snowmelt carrying winter away is an image of renewal, with no sense of uneasy waiting.
distractorExplanations.c: Children racing without coats is a cheerful image of spring arriving, not of anxious waiting.

sat-readiness-check-reading-and-writing-.prompt: A student is writing a report on the four-day school week. She claims that the schedule can help rural school districts keep their teachers. Which finding, if true, would most directly support the student's claim?

options.a: Rural districts that switched to four days lost fewer teachers over three years than similar five-day districts did.
options.b: Urban districts rarely adopt four-day weeks because many working families there struggle to arrange a fifth day of childcare.
options.c: Students in four-day districts spend slightly more time in class each school day than students in five-day districts.
options.d: Teachers in rural districts earn less on average than teachers in suburban and urban districts with similar experience.

sat-readiness-check-reading-and-writing-.explanation: The claim links the four-day schedule to teacher retention in rural districts. The finding that rural four-day districts lost fewer teachers than similar five-day districts directly compares retention under the two schedules.

distractorExplanations.b: This explains why urban districts avoid the schedule; it says nothing about rural teacher retention.
distractorExplanations.d: Lower rural pay may explain turnover, but it does not connect the four-day schedule to keeping teachers.
distractorExplanations.c: Daily class time concerns students, not whether teachers stay in their jobs.

sat-readiness-check-reading-and-writing-.prompt: Researchers hypothesized that a plant called sweet clover spreads quickly through prairies mainly because grazing animals avoid eating it, leaving it free to grow while native grasses are eaten. Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken the researchers' hypothesis?

options.a: Grazing animals in the study area ate native grasses far more often than they ate sweet clover.
options.b: Sweet clover was first brought to North American prairies as a crop for feeding cattle and sheep.
options.c: Sweet clover produces more seeds per plant than most native prairie grasses produce each season.
options.d: Sweet clover spreads just as quickly in fenced prairie plots where no grazing animals are present.

sat-readiness-check-reading-and-writing-.explanation: If grazing avoidance were the main reason, removing grazers should remove sweet clover's advantage. Fast spread in fenced plots with no grazers shows the plant spreads quickly without that advantage, which undercuts the hypothesis.

distractorExplanations.a: Grazers favoring native grasses supports the hypothesis rather than weakening it.
distractorExplanations.c: High seed output suggests another possible factor but does not show that grazing avoidance is unimportant.
distractorExplanations.b: How the plant arrived on prairies is historical background, not evidence about why it spreads.

sat-readiness-check-reading-and-writing-.prompt: In the novel The Lantern Keeper, the narrator's grandfather is portrayed as someone who values careful work over speed. Which quotation from the novel most effectively illustrates this portrayal?

options.a: "He sanded each oar three times, though one pass would have satisfied anyone else."
options.b: "Every morning he walked down to the harbor before the gulls were even awake."
options.c: "He laughed at the tourists who paid too much for postcards of the lighthouse."
options.d: "He kept his father's old compass in a drawer that he never seemed to open."

sat-readiness-check-reading-and-writing-.explanation: The portrayal is about choosing care over speed. Sanding each oar three times when one pass would satisfy others shows him spending extra time to do the job thoroughly.

distractorExplanations.b: Rising early shows a habit or routine, not careful work at the expense of speed.
distractorExplanations.d: Keeping a compass suggests sentiment or memory, not attention to the quality of his work.
distractorExplanations.c: Laughing at tourists reveals his humor or opinions, not how carefully he works.

sat-readiness-check-reading-and-writing-.prompt: Linguist Omar Haddad argues that bilingual children are better than monolingual children at noticing when a speaker's words are ambiguous, because switching between languages trains them to pay close attention to context. Which finding, if true, would most strongly support Haddad's argument?

options.a: Bilingual children learn to read at about the same age as monolingual children who attend the same elementary schools.
options.b: Monolingual students who begin a second language in high school say that grammar, not vocabulary, is the hardest part.
options.c: Given unclear instructions, bilingual children asked clarifying questions more often than monolingual children of the same age.
options.d: Bilingual adults are more likely than monolingual adults to hold jobs that require frequent international travel.

sat-readiness-check-reading-and-writing-.explanation: Haddad's argument is specifically about children noticing ambiguity. Bilingual children asking more clarifying questions when instructions are unclear is direct behavioral evidence that they notice ambiguity more than same-age monolingual peers.

distractorExplanations.a: Reading age is a different skill and shows no difference between the groups.
distractorExplanations.b: This concerns older learners' views of grammar, not bilingual children's attention to ambiguity.
distractorExplanations.d: Adult career patterns say nothing about children's ability to notice ambiguous speech.

sat-readiness-check-reading-and-writing-.formula:
| Town | Weekly recyclers, 2015 | Weekly recyclers, 2023 |
|---|---|---|
| Ashford | 38% | 71% |
| Bellmont | 52% | 74% |
| Carver | 45% | 69% |
| Dunmore | 60% | 78% |
sat-readiness-check-reading-and-writing-.prompt: A student researching household recycling compiled the table shown, which gives the percentage of households in four towns that recycled at least once a week in 2015 and in 2023. The student claims that Ashford had the largest increase in weekly recycling over that period. Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support the student's claim?

options.a: In 2023, Ashford had a higher share of households recycling weekly than any of the other three towns.
options.b: Dunmore had the highest share of households recycling weekly in both 2015 and 2023 among the four towns.
options.c: Weekly recycling in Ashford rose by 33 percentage points, a larger gain than in any of the other towns.
options.d: Bellmont's share of households recycling weekly rose from 52% in 2015 to 74% in 2023, a gain of 22 points.

sat-readiness-check-reading-and-writing-.explanation: The claim is about the largest increase, so the support must compare changes. Ashford rose 33 points (38% to 71%), versus 22 for Bellmont, 24 for Carver, and 18 for Dunmore, making Ashford's gain the largest.

distractorExplanations.a: False: Dunmore (78%) and Bellmont (74%) were higher than Ashford (71%) in 2023, and the claim concerns change, not level.
distractorExplanations.b: Accurate, but it describes Dunmore's levels and says nothing about which town increased the most.
distractorExplanations.d: Accurate for Bellmont, but one town's gain cannot show that Ashford's gain was the largest.

sat-readiness-check-reading-and-writing-.formula:
| Flower | Morning visits | Afternoon visits |
|---|---|---|
| Lavender | 42 | 67 |
| Clover | 58 | 31 |
| Thyme | 25 | 29 |
sat-readiness-check-reading-and-writing-.prompt: Ecologist Priya Nair counted bee visits to three kinds of flowers in a meadow during morning and afternoon observation periods; her results are shown in the table. She concluded that bees visited lavender more often in the afternoon than in the morning, while the reverse was true for clover. Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Nair's conclusion?

options.a: Clover received more morning visits than lavender did, and thyme received the fewest morning visits of the three flowers.
options.b: Thyme received 25 visits in the morning and 29 in the afternoon, a smaller change than for either of the other flowers.
options.c: Lavender received 67 visits in the afternoon, which is more than clover and thyme received combined in that period.
options.d: Lavender received 42 morning and 67 afternoon visits, whereas clover received 58 morning and 31 afternoon visits.

sat-readiness-check-reading-and-writing-.explanation: The conclusion has two halves: lavender afternoon > morning, and clover morning > afternoon. Only the choice giving both flowers' morning and afternoon counts (42 to 67; 58 to 31) supports both halves.

distractorExplanations.a: Compares flowers within the morning only; it never shows how either flower changed from morning to afternoon.
distractorExplanations.c: True (67 > 31 + 29), but it covers only the afternoon and ignores the clover half of the conclusion.
distractorExplanations.b: Thyme is not part of the conclusion, so its small change cannot support it.

sat-readiness-check-reading-and-writing-.formula:
| Primary source of local news | Ages 18–29 | Ages 30–49 | Ages 50+ |
|---|---|---|---|
| Social media | 46% | 31% | 14% |
| Television | 22% | 34% | 51% |
| Newspapers/websites | 32% | 35% | 35% |
sat-readiness-check-reading-and-writing-.prompt: A researcher surveyed adults about their primary source of local news; the results are shown in the table. The researcher claims that among adults aged 18–29, social media is a more common primary source of local news than television. Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support the claim?

options.a: Among adults aged 18–29, 46% named social media as their primary source, compared with 22% who named television.
options.b: Among adults aged 50 and older, 51% named television as their primary source, compared with 14% for social media.
options.c: Adults aged 30–49 were about equally likely to name social media or newspapers and websites as their primary source.
options.d: Newspapers and websites were named by roughly a third of adults in every one of the age groups that were surveyed.

sat-readiness-check-reading-and-writing-.explanation: The claim concerns only adults aged 18–29 and compares social media with television. The choice citing 46% for social media versus 22% for television in that age group is the only one that addresses the claim directly.

distractorExplanations.c: Describes adults aged 30–49 and compares the wrong two sources.
distractorExplanations.d: Accurate, but it concerns newspapers and websites, which are not part of the claim.
distractorExplanations.b: Describes the wrong age group, and in that group television, not social media, is more common.

sat-readiness-check-reading-and-writing-.formula:
| Water temperature | Average dissolving time |
|---|---|
| 20°C | 96 seconds |
| 40°C | 61 seconds |
| 60°C | 41 seconds |
| 80°C | 30 seconds |
sat-readiness-check-reading-and-writing-.prompt: Students tested how water temperature affects how quickly sugar dissolves; their results are shown in the table. They claim that raising the water temperature from 20°C to 60°C more than halved the average dissolving time. Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support the claim?

options.a: At 40°C the sugar dissolved in 61 seconds on average, which is 35 seconds faster than it dissolved at 20°C.
options.b: At 80°C the sugar dissolved in 30 seconds on average, the shortest time recorded at any of the four temperatures.
options.c: At 60°C the sugar dissolved in 41 seconds on average, which is only 11 seconds slower than it dissolved at 80°C.
options.d: At 20°C the sugar took 96 seconds on average, but at 60°C it took 41 seconds, less than half as long.

sat-readiness-check-reading-and-writing-.explanation: 'More than halved' compares the 20°C and 60°C times. Half of 96 seconds is 48 seconds, and 41 seconds is less than that, so the choice citing both values is the only one that supports the claim.

distractorExplanations.a: Accurate, but 40°C is not the temperature named in the claim, so it cannot show the time was halved at 60°C.
distractorExplanations.b: Accurate, but 80°C is outside the 20°C to 60°C comparison the claim makes.
distractorExplanations.c: Compares 60°C with 80°C instead of with 20°C, so it does not address halving.

sat-readiness-check-reading-and-writing-.prompt: Archaeologists excavating a 3,000-year-old village found grinding stones, storage pits filled with charred barley, and sickle blades with a glossy polish that forms when stone repeatedly cuts grass stems. However, they found no bones of domesticated animals at the site. These findings suggest that the villagers ______ Which choice most logically completes the text?

options.a: raised cattle and sheep but traded with neighboring villages for all of their grain.
options.b: used their sickle blades mainly for hunting wild animals rather than for farming.
options.c: abandoned the village after a fire destroyed their entire supply of stored barley.
options.d: relied on harvesting and processing grain but may not have kept livestock.

sat-readiness-check-reading-and-writing-.explanation: Grinding stones, stored barley, and grass-polished sickles all point to harvesting and processing grain; the absence of domesticated animal bones suggests no livestock. The hedge 'may not have' fits evidence based on what was not found.

distractorExplanations.a: Contradicts the evidence: no livestock bones were found, and the grain tools show grain was processed on site.
distractorExplanations.c: Charred barley does not prove a fire forced the villagers to leave; the text never mentions abandonment.
distractorExplanations.b: The polish forms from cutting grass stems, which points to harvesting, not hunting.

sat-readiness-check-reading-and-writing-.prompt: Some astronomers have proposed that an undiscovered ninth planet explains why the orbits of several small icy bodies beyond Neptune appear clustered together. Other astronomers note that those bodies were found by surveys that searched only certain parts of the sky, where objects with clustered orbits happen to be easier to detect. If the second group is correct, then the apparent clustering ______ Which choice most logically completes the text?

options.a: proves that a ninth planet must lie in the parts of the sky that have not yet been surveyed.
options.b: was caused by Neptune's gravity pulling the small icy bodies into very similar orbits.
options.c: may reflect where astronomers happened to look rather than the pull of an unseen planet.
options.d: will disappear entirely once telescopes are pointed at the same regions of the sky again.

sat-readiness-check-reading-and-writing-.explanation: The second group's point is a sampling problem: surveys looked where clustered objects are easier to find. If that is right, the clustering could be an artifact of where astronomers searched, not evidence of a planet's gravity.

distractorExplanations.a: Reverses the second group's point, which casts doubt on the planet rather than proving it.
distractorExplanations.b: Introduces Neptune's gravity, an explanation neither group in the text proposes.
distractorExplanations.d: Searching the same regions again would repeat the bias, not remove it.

sat-readiness-check-reading-and-writing-.prompt: When a mid-sized city began offering free public transit on weekends, weekend ridership nearly doubled. Weekday ridership, which still required a fare, did not change. City officials therefore concluded that ______ Which choice most logically completes the text?

options.a: the cost of fares had been discouraging some residents from riding on weekends.
options.b: weekday riders had switched to traveling on weekends in order to avoid paying fares.
options.c: free transit should end because it had caused serious crowding on weekday buses.
options.d: most residents prefer to drive on weekdays because the city's buses are too slow.

sat-readiness-check-reading-and-writing-.explanation: Removing the fare on weekends doubled weekend ridership while fare-paying weekday ridership stayed flat. The logical conclusion is that the fare itself had been keeping some people from riding on weekends.

distractorExplanations.c: The text reports no weekday crowding; weekday ridership stayed the same.
distractorExplanations.d: Bus speed and driving habits are never discussed, so this conclusion has no support.
distractorExplanations.b: If weekday riders had switched, weekday ridership would have fallen, but it did not change.

sat-readiness-check-reading-and-writing-.prompt: In laboratory tests, a new coating kept bridge steel from rusting for the equivalent of 40 years of exposure to rain and road salt. The tests did not, however, include the repeated freezing and thawing that bridges in cold climates undergo, a process that can crack protective coatings. Thus, the test results can most reasonably be applied to ______ Which choice most logically completes the text?

options.a: bridges in mild climates with more confidence than to bridges in cold climates.
options.b: every bridge, since the coating is certain to crack within a few years anyway.
options.c: bridges anywhere, because road salt no longer poses a threat to coated steel.
options.d: bridges in cold climates, where the coating should outperform other coatings.

sat-readiness-check-reading-and-writing-.explanation: The tests covered rain and salt but not freeze-thaw cycles, which can crack coatings. The results therefore fit conditions that resemble the tests (mild climates) better than cold climates, where an untested stress applies.

distractorExplanations.b: Overstates the limitation: the text says freezing can crack coatings, not that this coating will crack everywhere.
distractorExplanations.c: Ignores the stated gap in the testing and overgeneralizes the results to all conditions.
distractorExplanations.d: Reverses the logic: cold climates are exactly where the results are least reliable.

sat-readiness-check-reading-and-writing-.prompt: A bakery tested two versions of its online menu. Version A listed each pastry's price first, and Version B listed each pastry's description first. Customers who saw Version B ordered more items per visit, even though the prices and pastries were identical in both versions. This result suggests that ______ Which choice most logically completes the text?

options.a: customers who saw Version A were unable to find the prices of the pastries.
options.b: Version B offered a larger selection of pastries than Version A offered.
options.c: the bakery should raise its prices because customers rarely notice them.
options.d: the way the menu presented information influenced how much customers bought.

sat-readiness-check-reading-and-writing-.explanation: Only the order of information differed between the menus, yet Version B led to more items per visit. The logical inference is that presentation affected buying behavior.

distractorExplanations.a: Version A listed prices first, so prices were easy to find; nothing suggests customers missed them.
distractorExplanations.c: The test did not change prices, so it gives no basis for a recommendation about raising them.
distractorExplanations.b: Contradicts the text, which says the pastries were identical in both versions.

sat-readiness-check-reading-and-writing-.prompt: The museum's new exhibit is deliberately ______: rather than filling the hall with hundreds of objects, the curators chose just twelve, each displayed on its own wall. Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word?

options.a: crowded
options.b: temporary
options.c: sparse
options.d: expensive

sat-readiness-check-reading-and-writing-.explanation: The colon signals that the second half explains the blank: only twelve objects, each on its own wall, instead of hundreds. 'Sparse' (thinly filled) is the word that matches that description.

distractorExplanations.a: 'Crowded' is the opposite of an exhibit with only twelve widely spaced objects.
distractorExplanations.b: Nothing in the text describes how long the exhibit will last.
distractorExplanations.d: The text gives no information about the exhibit's cost.

sat-readiness-check-reading-and-writing-.prompt: Although critics initially dismissed the composer's early symphonies as derivative, later scholars have argued that the works are surprisingly ______, introducing harmonies that no earlier composer had attempted. Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word?

options.a: innovative
options.b: conventional
options.c: repetitive
options.d: popular

sat-readiness-check-reading-and-writing-.explanation: 'Although' sets up a contrast with 'derivative' (copying others), and the blank is explained by harmonies 'no earlier composer had attempted.' 'Innovative' fits both the contrast and the explanation.

distractorExplanations.c: 'Repetitive' does not match introducing harmonies never attempted before.
distractorExplanations.d: Popularity is unrelated to the contrast between derivative and new harmonies.
distractorExplanations.b: 'Conventional' agrees with the critics' view instead of contrasting with it.

sat-readiness-check-reading-and-writing-.prompt: Marine biologist Keiko Ota cautions that a single unusually warm year does not ______ a long-term trend; only decades of temperature records can show whether ocean conditions are truly shifting. Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word?

options.a: obscure
options.b: reverse
options.c: contradict
options.d: establish

sat-readiness-check-reading-and-writing-.explanation: Ota's point is that one warm year is not enough evidence; decades of records are needed to show a trend. 'Establish' (prove or demonstrate) captures that one data point cannot prove a long-term pattern.

distractorExplanations.a: A warm year would not hide a warming trend, and the second clause is about proving a trend, not hiding one.
distractorExplanations.c: A warm year would be consistent with warming, so 'contradict' misses the point about evidence.
distractorExplanations.b: Nothing suggests a single year could reverse a trend; the issue is how much evidence is needed.

sat-readiness-check-reading-and-writing-.prompt: The novelist's prose is notably ______: she rarely uses two words where one will do, and many of her chapters run only a page or two. Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word?

options.a: florid
options.b: whimsical
options.c: ambiguous
options.d: terse

sat-readiness-check-reading-and-writing-.explanation: The colon introduces the evidence: few words and very short chapters. 'Terse' means brief and using few words, which matches exactly.

distractorExplanations.a: 'Florid' means elaborate and heavily ornamented, the opposite of using as few words as possible.
distractorExplanations.b: 'Whimsical' means playful or fanciful, which says nothing about brevity.
distractorExplanations.c: 'Ambiguous' means unclear in meaning; short prose is not necessarily unclear.

sat-readiness-check-reading-and-writing-.prompt: Early settlers planted long rows of cottonwood trees along the river to check the spread of sand dunes that threatened their fields. As used in the text, what does the word "check" most nearly mean?

options.a: limit
options.b: examine
options.c: approve
options.d: record

sat-readiness-check-reading-and-writing-.explanation: Trees were planted because dunes 'threatened their fields,' so the settlers wanted to hold back the dunes. In this context 'check' means to limit or restrain, not to inspect.

distractorExplanations.c: The settlers wanted to stop the dunes, not approve of them.
distractorExplanations.d: Trees cannot record the dunes' spread; they physically hold the sand back.
distractorExplanations.b: 'Examine' is a common meaning of 'check,' but planting trees does not inspect dunes.

sat-readiness-check-reading-and-writing-.prompt: The committee's report described the funding shortfall as a grave matter that would require immediate action from the city council. As used in the text, what does the word "grave" most nearly mean?

options.a: quiet
options.b: buried
options.c: deliberate
options.d: serious

sat-readiness-check-reading-and-writing-.explanation: A problem that 'would require immediate action' is an important, worrying one. Here 'grave' is an adjective meaning serious, not the noun for a burial place.

distractorExplanations.a: 'Grave' can describe a quiet, solemn manner, but a shortfall demanding immediate action is not 'quiet.'
distractorExplanations.b: Plays on the noun 'grave' (a burial site), which does not fit an adjective describing a matter.
distractorExplanations.c: 'Deliberate' means intentional; the text does not say the shortfall was planned.

sat-readiness-check-reading-and-writing-.prompt: In her study of medieval trade routes, historian Inés Calvo shows that merchants did not simply carry goods; they also ______ ideas, spreading new farming methods and mathematical techniques from one region to another. Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word?

options.a: concealed
options.b: fabricated
options.c: conveyed
options.d: rejected

sat-readiness-check-reading-and-writing-.explanation: The blank is explained by 'spreading new farming methods and mathematical techniques from one region to another.' 'Conveyed' (passed along, transmitted) matches merchants carrying ideas as well as goods.

distractorExplanations.a: Merchants who hid ideas could not spread them to other regions.
distractorExplanations.b: 'Fabricated' means invented or made up; the text says merchants spread existing methods.
distractorExplanations.d: Rejecting ideas is the opposite of spreading them.

sat-readiness-check-reading-and-writing-.prompt: The scientist's claims were ______ by the new data: measurements from three independent laboratories matched her original predictions almost exactly. Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word?

options.a: undermined
options.b: overshadowed
options.c: complicated
options.d: confirmed

sat-readiness-check-reading-and-writing-.explanation: Independent measurements that 'matched her original predictions almost exactly' support her claims. 'Confirmed' is the only choice that means the data backed the claims up.

distractorExplanations.a: 'Undermined' means weakened, but matching data strengthens the claims.
distractorExplanations.c: Data that match predictions almost exactly make the picture clearer, not more complicated.
distractorExplanations.b: Nothing in the text suggests the claims were pushed aside by something more important.

sat-readiness-check-reading-and-writing-.prompt: Because the trail's steepest sections had been ______ with switchbacks, even young children were able to reach the summit without much difficulty. Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word?

options.a: blocked
options.b: hidden
options.c: eased
options.d: abandoned

sat-readiness-check-reading-and-writing-.explanation: 'Because' links the blank to the result that young children reached the summit easily. Switchbacks make a steep slope gentler, so the sections were 'eased.'

distractorExplanations.a: Blocked sections would stop hikers rather than help children reach the summit.
distractorExplanations.b: Hiding the steep sections would not make the climb any easier.
distractorExplanations.d: If the sections were abandoned, the trail would not lead to the summit at all.

sat-readiness-check-reading-and-writing-.prompt: Some readers find the poet's later work ______, but its difficulty is deliberate: she wanted readers to slow down and puzzle over each line. Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word?

options.a: opaque
options.b: sentimental
options.c: cheerful
options.d: predictable

sat-readiness-check-reading-and-writing-.explanation: The phrase 'its difficulty is deliberate' refers back to the blank, so the blank must describe difficulty. 'Opaque' means hard to understand, which matches readers having to puzzle over each line.

distractorExplanations.b: 'Sentimental' describes emotional tone, not difficulty of understanding.
distractorExplanations.c: 'Cheerful' describes mood and does not connect to the poem being difficult.
distractorExplanations.d: Predictable writing would be easy to follow, the opposite of work readers must puzzle over.

sat-readiness-check-reading-and-writing-.prompt: Most hummingbirds lower their body temperature at night to save energy. The black metaltail, a hummingbird of the Andes, takes this further: on cold nights its body temperature can drop to about 3°C, among the lowest ever recorded for a bird. By morning, it rewarms and resumes feeding. Which choice best describes the function of the second sentence in the overall structure of the text?

options.a: It presents an extreme example of the behavior described in the first sentence.
options.b: It introduces a claim about hummingbird metabolism that the final sentence disputes.
options.c: It explains why hummingbirds that live in the Andes need to save energy at night.
options.d: It contrasts hummingbirds with other birds that stay warm throughout the night.

sat-readiness-check-reading-and-writing-.explanation: The first sentence states a general behavior (lowering body temperature at night). The second, signaled by 'takes this further,' gives the black metaltail as an extreme case of that same behavior.

distractorExplanations.b: The final sentence describes what happens next (rewarming); it does not dispute anything.
distractorExplanations.c: The sentence describes how far the temperature drops, not why Andean birds need to save energy.
distractorExplanations.d: No other birds are compared; the sentence compares one hummingbird with most hummingbirds.

sat-readiness-check-reading-and-writing-.prompt: In the late 1800s, Chicago faced a serious problem: sewage flowing into the Chicago River ran into Lake Michigan, the source of the city's drinking water. Engineers responded with an ambitious plan to reverse the river's flow so that it would carry waste away from the lake and toward the Mississippi River basin. The canal that achieved this, completed in 1900, was one of the largest earthmoving projects of its time. Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?

options.a: To argue that reversing the Chicago River created new problems for cities downstream
options.b: To compare Chicago's water system with the systems of other cities on Lake Michigan
options.c: To describe a problem Chicago faced and the engineering project designed to solve it
options.d: To explain why Lake Michigan became the main source of drinking water for Chicago

sat-readiness-check-reading-and-writing-.explanation: The text names a problem (sewage reaching the drinking-water source) and then describes the solution (reversing the river with a canal). Its purpose is to describe that problem and the engineering response.

distractorExplanations.a: The text makes no argument about downstream effects; it simply describes the project.
distractorExplanations.b: No other cities are mentioned, so there is no comparison.
distractorExplanations.d: The text states that the lake was the water source but never explains why.

sat-readiness-check-reading-and-writing-.prompt: The following text is from a short story. Grandmother kept the letters in a tin that had once held peppermints, and though the candy was decades gone, a faint sweetness still rose whenever she lifted the lid. She never read the letters aloud. She only touched their edges, as if counting them, and then set the tin back on the high shelf. Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?

options.a: To explain why the grandmother refuses to let her family read the letters in the tin
options.b: To describe how the grandmother came to own a tin that had once held peppermints
options.c: To convey, through her careful handling, how much the letters privately mean to her
options.d: To show that the grandmother has forgotten who wrote the letters and what they say

sat-readiness-check-reading-and-writing-.explanation: The text never states her feelings; it shows them through ritual-like handling: touching the edges, counting, returning the tin to a high shelf. Its purpose is to suggest the letters' private importance to her.

distractorExplanations.a: The text never mentions her family asking to read the letters or her refusing.
distractorExplanations.b: The tin's past use as a peppermint box is a detail; how she got it is never explained.
distractorExplanations.d: Nothing suggests forgetting; her careful handling points to how much the letters matter.

sat-readiness-check-reading-and-writing-.prompt: Many people believe that the Great Wall of China can be seen with the naked eye from the Moon. The wall is long but narrow, rarely more than about 9 meters wide, and its color blends with the surrounding land. Astronauts who have looked for it from low Earth orbit report that it is hard to pick out even there, let alone from the Moon, roughly 384,000 kilometers away. Which choice best describes the function of the final sentence in the text as a whole?

options.a: It offers firsthand evidence that undermines the belief stated in the first sentence.
options.b: It explains why the wall's builders chose materials that blend in with the land around it.
options.c: It suggests that astronauts in low orbit have helped scientists measure the wall's width.
options.d: It introduces a new belief about the wall that the rest of the text goes on to support.

sat-readiness-check-reading-and-writing-.explanation: The first sentence states a popular belief, and the final sentence reports astronauts' own observations that the wall is hard to see even from much closer than the Moon. That firsthand evidence undercuts the belief.

distractorExplanations.c: The astronauts tried to see the wall; the text does not say they measured it.
distractorExplanations.d: It is the last sentence, so nothing follows it, and it challenges a belief rather than introducing one.
distractorExplanations.b: The text mentions the wall's color but never discusses why builders chose their materials.

sat-readiness-check-reading-and-writing-.prompt: For much of the twentieth century, scientists believed that the adult human brain could not grow new neurons. In the 1990s, researchers reported new neurons forming in the adult hippocampus, a region linked to memory. Since then, some studies have questioned how common such growth really is in humans, and the debate continues. Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?

options.a: It describes a discovery, explains how it was used to treat memory loss, and then evaluates the results.
options.b: It outlines a theory, presents evidence that confirmed it, and explains why it is now universally accepted.
options.c: It compares two regions of the brain and argues that one is more important for memory than the other.
options.d: It presents a long-held belief, describes findings that challenged it, and notes that the issue is still disputed.

sat-readiness-check-reading-and-writing-.explanation: The text moves in three steps: the old belief (no new adult neurons), the 1990s findings that challenged it, and later studies that keep the question open. Only this choice tracks all three steps in order.

distractorExplanations.a: The text mentions no treatment for memory loss.
distractorExplanations.c: Only one brain region is named, and no comparison of importance is made.
distractorExplanations.b: The text ends with an ongoing debate, the opposite of universal acceptance.

sat-readiness-check-reading-and-writing-.prompt: Tiny glass beads mixed into road paint make lane markings shine in headlights at night. Each bead acts like a small lens, bending the light that enters it and sending it back toward the driver instead of scattering it in all directions. Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?

options.a: To argue that roads should use brighter paint instead of relying on glass beads
options.b: To describe the history of how lane markings were first painted on roads
options.c: To compare the safety of driving at night with driving during the day
options.d: To explain how a common material makes road markings visible at night

sat-readiness-check-reading-and-writing-.explanation: Both sentences explain a mechanism: beads act as lenses that send headlight light back to the driver. The purpose is explanatory, showing how the beads make markings visible at night.

distractorExplanations.a: The text makes no argument for replacing the beads; it explains how they work.
distractorExplanations.b: No history of lane markings is given.
distractorExplanations.c: Daytime driving is never mentioned, so there is no comparison.

sat-readiness-check-reading-and-writing-.prompt: The following text is from a short story. The storm had passed by dawn. Nell walked the length of the orchard, counting the broken branches and the apples scattered in the wet grass. At the far end, the oldest tree stood untouched, its fruit still hanging, as though the night had simply forgotten it. Which choice best describes the function of the final sentence in the text as a whole?

options.a: It explains why the storm caused far less damage than Nell had expected it to cause.
options.b: It contrasts a single spared tree with the damage described in the preceding sentence.
options.c: It reveals that Nell planted the orchard's oldest tree herself many years before.
options.d: It suggests that Nell plans to harvest the remaining apples later that morning.

sat-readiness-check-reading-and-writing-.explanation: The second sentence lists damage (broken branches, fallen apples); the final sentence presents the oldest tree 'untouched.' Its role is to contrast that one spared tree with the surrounding damage.

distractorExplanations.a: The text never says what damage Nell expected, and it describes plenty of damage.
distractorExplanations.c: Nothing in the text says who planted the tree.
distractorExplanations.d: No plans to harvest are mentioned; the sentence describes the tree, not Nell's intentions.

sat-readiness-check-reading-and-writing-.prompt: Researchers often study animal intelligence by testing whether animals can use tools. Yet some scientists warn that this focus can overlook skills that matter more for a species' survival. A bird that never uses a stick to reach food may still remember hundreds of places where it has hidden seeds, a feat that requires remarkable memory. Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?

options.a: To argue that birds are more intelligent than any other animals that use tools
options.b: To describe a new experiment that tested birds' ability to find hidden seeds
options.c: To explain why animals that use tools are more likely to survive in the wild
options.d: To suggest that tool use is too narrow a measure of how intelligent an animal is

sat-readiness-check-reading-and-writing-.explanation: The text raises a concern about relying on tool-use tests and gives an example of an important skill (memory) that such tests would miss. Its purpose is to suggest tool use is too narrow a measure of intelligence.

distractorExplanations.a: The text makes no ranking of birds against other animals.
distractorExplanations.b: The seed-hiding bird is a general example, not a description of a specific experiment.
distractorExplanations.c: The text suggests other skills may matter more for survival, not that tool users survive better.

sat-readiness-check-reading-and-writing-.prompt: Text 1: Many nutrition guides recommend eating breakfast every day, citing studies in which people who ate breakfast weighed less than people who skipped it. Text 2: Nutrition researcher Alan Koh points out that most of those studies were observational: they compared people who already ate breakfast with people who did not. When Koh's team randomly assigned adults to eat or skip breakfast for sixteen weeks, the two groups lost about the same amount of weight. Based on the texts, how would Koh (Text 2) most likely respond to the guides discussed in Text 1?

options.a: By agreeing that eating breakfast every day is the most effective way to lose weight
options.b: By arguing that their advice rests on studies that cannot show breakfast causes weight loss
options.c: By claiming that skipping breakfast causes people to gain weight over sixteen weeks
options.d: By suggesting that the guides should recommend a larger lunch instead of breakfast

sat-readiness-check-reading-and-writing-.explanation: Koh's point is methodological: observational studies only compare existing habits, so they cannot prove cause. His randomized trial found no difference, so he would say the guides' advice is not supported by causal evidence.

distractorExplanations.a: Koh's trial found no weight difference between eaters and skippers, so he would not agree.
distractorExplanations.c: Both groups lost about the same amount of weight, so skipping did not cause weight gain.
distractorExplanations.d: Koh says nothing about lunch; the texts are only about breakfast.

sat-readiness-check-reading-and-writing-.prompt: Text 1: Historian Ruth Abara argues that the printing press spread new ideas in sixteenth-century Europe chiefly because it made books cheaper, so that more people could afford to read controversial works. Text 2: Historian Paul Ferrante agrees that cheaper books mattered, but he emphasizes that printed pamphlets were often read aloud in taverns and town squares, reaching many people who could not read at all. Based on the texts, how would Ferrante most likely respond to Abara's argument?

options.a: By rejecting the idea that printed books became cheaper in the sixteenth century
options.b: By arguing that taverns mattered more than the printing press in spreading ideas
options.c: By noting that printed works also spread ideas among people who never read them
options.d: By claiming that most people in sixteenth-century Europe could read controversial works

sat-readiness-check-reading-and-writing-.explanation: Ferrante accepts Abara's point about cheaper books but adds another channel: pamphlets read aloud to people who could not read. He would extend her argument by noting that print reached non-readers too.

distractorExplanations.a: Ferrante 'agrees that cheaper books mattered,' so he does not reject that point.
distractorExplanations.b: Taverns were where printed pamphlets were read; Ferrante does not rank them above the press.
distractorExplanations.d: Ferrante stresses that many people 'could not read at all,' the opposite of this claim.

sat-readiness-check-reading-and-writing-.prompt: Text 1: Some city planners argue that adding lanes to busy highways reduces traffic jams by giving cars more room. Text 2: Transportation researcher Mei Lin describes a pattern called induced demand: when highways are widened, driving becomes easier, so more people choose to drive, and within a few years congestion often returns to its earlier level. Based on the texts, how would Lin (Text 2) most likely respond to the planners in Text 1?

options.a: She would agree that widening highways is the best long-term solution to congestion.
options.b: She would argue that highways should be narrowed so that fewer people choose to drive.
options.c: She would argue that any relief gained by adding lanes is likely to be temporary.
options.d: She would claim that adding lanes makes highways more dangerous for most drivers.

sat-readiness-check-reading-and-writing-.explanation: Induced demand means wider highways attract more drivers until congestion 'returns to its earlier level.' Lin would therefore say the planners' relief is real at first but likely temporary.

distractorExplanations.a: Lin's pattern shows congestion returning, so she would not call widening the best long-term fix.
distractorExplanations.b: Lin describes what happens after widening; she does not propose narrowing highways.
distractorExplanations.d: Safety is never discussed in either text.
